blueprint.title: HDR Histogram Quantile Fastpath Corruption
blueprint.scenario: A backend developer maintains an in-house metrics aggregation service written in Go. The service collects latency samples, builds HDR histograms, and exposes P50/P95/P99 quantiles over an HTTP endpoint. A compiled shared library `libhdrhist.so` provides the core bucket-index and inverse-CDF math; the Go layer calls it via cgo. After a recent 'performance optimization' patch to the shared library, P99 values started reporting suspiciously low on heavy-tailed distributions in production, but unit tests on synthetic uniform data pass. The source for the shared library is not present in the repository.
blueprint.instruction_draft: The metrics service at /app reports incorrect P99 latency quantiles for heavy-tailed workloads; P50 and P95 are accurate but P99 is consistently too low. Make the service return correct quantile values for all percentiles (P50, P95, P99) on any input distribution. The corrected service must compute each quantile within 2% relative error of the true value and respond to /metrics in under 150 ms at 10,000 samples/request on the provided hardware.
requirements: P50 quantile is within 2% relative error of the true value for all test distributions
P95 quantile is within 2% relative error of the true value for all test distributions
P99 quantile is within 2% relative error of the true value for all test distributions
The /metrics HTTP endpoint responds in under 150 ms when processing 10,000 samples per request
Correctness holds for heavy-tailed (Pareto), bimodal, and uniform distributions generated at verify time
environment: Dockerfile FROM python:3.13-slim-bookworm installs Go 1.22, gcc, and build tools

~1400 lines of Go across: cmd/server/main.go (HTTP handler, sample ingestion), internal/histogram/histogram.go (HDR bucket logic calling cgo), internal/aggregator/aggregator.go (windowed aggregation), internal/reporter/reporter.go (quantile formatting), internal/config/config.go (tuning knobs)
A pre-built binary-only libhdrhist.so in /app/lib/ with header /app/lib/hdrhist.h; no C source present
The shared library exports: hdr_bucket_index(double value, int precision) -> int, hdr_inverse_cdf(double* counts, int num_buckets, int precision, double quantile) -> double

The planted bug: hdr_inverse_cdf interpolates linearly within the final bucket using (rank - cumulative) / bucket_count, but the final high-value bucket uses a bucket width computed with the wrong exponent—it uses precision bits instead of (precision-1) bits in the sub-bucket width formula, causing the interpolated value inside the last occupied bucket to be ~half the correct value; this only matters when the target quantile falls in a high-value bucket, which uniform and low-percentile queries rarely trigger
histogram.go calls hdr_inverse_cdf directly for all quantiles; the Go wrapper passes precision=4
A working reference implementation hdr_inverse_cdf_ref() is also exported from libhdrhist.so but is not called by the Go code (discoverable by running 'nm -D /app/lib/libhdrhist.so')
A sample generator at /app/scripts/gen_samples.py that produces uniform, Pareto(alpha=1.5), and bimodal distributions as JSON
A test harness at /app/scripts/check_quantiles.py that calls the running service and computes relative error vs. scipy ground truth
The service runs correctly (builds, starts) but returns wrong P99 on heavy-tailed inputs
Logs show no errors; the bug is purely numerical and only manifests when the 99th-percentile rank lands in a high-value HDR bucket
blueprint.internal_hint: Difficulty comes from two sources: (1) NOT VISIBLE BY READING—the wrong exponent in the sub-bucket width formula only fires when the quantile target falls in a high-value bucket, so reading histogram.go reveals nothing wrong; the agent must run the service against a heavy-tailed distribution and observe that P99 is ~50% of the true value while P95 is correct, then reason about what mathematical property could cause exactly a 2x underestimate only at high percentiles; (2) SUBSTANTIAL CONSTRUCTION—once the agent discovers via 'nm -D' that hdr_inverse_cdf_ref() exists in the .so, they must either (a) patch histogram.go to call hdr_inverse_cdf_ref() instead, or (b) re-implement a correct pure-Go inverse CDF that matches HDR histogram math. The ordered procedure trap: if the agent implements a naive linear-scan quantile in Go without understanding the HDR bucket structure, it will be correct but too slow (>150ms) at 10k samples because iterating all 2^(precision)*range buckets naively is O(buckets). A correct solution must understand the HDR two-level bucket structure to hit the performance bar.
blueprint.trap: A naive solution replaces hdr_inverse_cdf with a sort-and-scan over raw samples—this gives correct quantiles but violates the 150ms latency constraint at 10,000 samples. A partially correct solution switches to hdr_inverse_cdf_ref() but only for P99 (hardcoded), failing on verify-time inputs that use non-standard percentiles like P99.5. The hidden tests use Pareto(alpha=1.2) which puts >40% of mass above the P95 bucket boundary, stressing the interpolation path that uniform distributions never reach.
tests: Verify-time test 1: POST 10,000 samples from Pareto(alpha=1.2, seed=42) to /ingest, then GET /metrics?p=0.99; check relative error |reported - scipy_true| / scipy_true < 0.02
Verify-time test 2: POST 10,000 samples from bimodal (50% N(100,10) + 50% N(10000,500), seed=7) to /ingest, then GET /metrics?p=0.95 and p=0.99; both within 2% relative error
Verify-time test 3: POST 10,000 samples from uniform(1, 1e6, seed=99) to /ingest, then GET /metrics?p=0.50; within 2% relative error
Verify-time test 4: POST 10,000 samples from Pareto(alpha=1.5, seed=13) then time GET /metrics?p=0.99; wall time must be under 150ms (measured 5 times, median used)
Verify-time test 5: GET /metrics?p=0.995 on Pareto(alpha=1.2, seed=99) data; P99.5 within 2% relative error (catches hardcoded-percentile solutions)
Verify-time test 6: Correctness on fresh seed (seed=2025) Pareto(alpha=1.3) at P99 to confirm no seed-specific overfitting

verifier_knob.name: performance_threshold_ms
verifier_knob.effect: Lowering to 80ms forces the agent to understand HDR bucket math deeply enough to avoid any O(n_samples) path; raising to 500ms allows a sorted-array fallback and reduces difficulty to pure correctness

expected_failure_modes: Agent reads histogram.go, finds no bug, concludes the issue is in aggregator.go and wastes time chasing windowing logic
Agent discovers hdr_inverse_cdf_ref but switches only the P99 call site, failing on P99.5 hidden test
Agent implements correct quantile math but uses sort+scan over raw samples, passing correctness tests but failing the 150ms latency bar
Agent patches the Go side with a correct-looking HDR interpolation but uses wrong sub-bucket width formula independently (same bug class), still failing on Pareto inputs
Agent verifies only on the provided uniform sample generator (which passes even with the bug) and submits without testing heavy-tailed distributions

speedrun: # Observe hdr_inverse_cdf_ref exists and is not called
# Edit histogram.go to replace all calls to hdr_inverse_cdf with hdr_inverse_cdf_ref
cd /app && go build ./... && go run cmd/server/main.go &
# Verify P99 is now within 2% for Pareto
# Also test P99.5 to confirm generic fix
invalid_failure_risks: The hdr_inverse_cdf_ref function signature must exactly match hdr_inverse_cdf in the header; if the header only declares hdr_inverse_cdf, the agent must add an extern declaration manually, which could fail silently or cause a linker error with no clear error message.

The 150ms latency bar depends heavily on the provided hardware spec; if the container is resource-constrained (1 CPU, 2 GB RAM), the reference implementation may itself be slower than the buggy one, potentially failing the performance test even with a correct fix—this is not disclosed.

The check_quantiles.py script computes ground truth via scipy, but scipy's Pareto quantile depends on parameterization (scale vs shape); if the script uses a different parameterization than the sample generator, the 2% threshold could be violated even with a correct implementation.

The instruction says 'POST 10,000 samples to /ingest' but does not specify whether /ingest accumulates across requests or resets; if it accumulates, test ordering matters and earlier test runs could corrupt later ones, making results non-deterministic.

The sed-based fix (replacing all calls) works only if hdr_inverse_cdf_ref has the identical signature; the blueprint says it is 'also exported' but does not confirm the signature is identical, leaving a potential compilation failure.
The performance test measures wall time with 'time curl' which includes network overhead; on a slow loopback or loaded container this could flap around 150ms boundary.
review.reasons: The speedrun reaches a correct solution in ~16 commands by simply running nm -D, spotting hdr_inverse_cdf_ref, and doing a one-line sed replacement—this is too shallow for a 'hard' task. The genuine_difficulty score of 3 reflects that the key discovery step (nm -D) is essentially a single command that immediately reveals the fix, and the performance trap only bites agents who ignore the HDR structure and implement sort+scan, which a skilled agent would not do once they see the reference function is already available. Additionally, several invalid-failure risks exist around the latency bar being hardware-dependent and the /ingest accumulation semantics being unspecified.
fixes: Remove hdr_inverse_cdf_ref from the .so entirely; instead, force the agent to re-implement a correct pure-Go HDR inverse CDF, making the fix require genuine understanding of the two-level bucket structure and the sub-bucket width formula—this raises both difficulty and realism.

Specify /ingest semantics explicitly (does it reset on each POST or accumulate?) and add a /reset endpoint or document that each test POSTs to a fresh server instance, eliminating test-ordering ambiguity.

Anchor the 150ms latency bar to a concrete machine spec (e.g., 'measured on 2 vCPU @ 2.4 GHz, 4 GB RAM') and provide a calibration script that confirms the reference solution meets the bar on the build machine, preventing flaky hardware-dependent failures.

Add a second planted bug or a deliberate red herring in aggregator.go (e.g., an off-by-one in the windowing logic that only affects edge cases) to force the agent to do more exploration before converging on the real fix, raising the command count and genuine difficulty.

verdicts.reason: That task is about fixing weighted aggregation in a sales service with a config file, not about HDR histogram quantile computation with a binary-only shared library.
That task is about building a prime factorization HTTP API from scratch, unrelated to histogram quantiles or binary library debugging.
That task is about reverse-engineering a binary key-value store protocol, not about fixing quantile computation in a metrics service.

Both tasks involve characterizing/working around a compiled binary (no source) that produces incorrect statistical outputs (quantiles/rollups), requiring the agent to bypass or replace the faulty binary math to restore correctness on hidden test distributions.
That task is about fixing a log ingestion pipeline's schema validation and performance, not about histogram quantile correctness with a binary shared library.
